questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Well, every experience abroad is also contingent on the specifics of the person abroad's life and i think my experiences on the trip abroad was fine, but i was unlucky and didn't meet anyone i wanted to spend a lot of time with during the trip. This is a big part of what is bringing the score down. 

Another aspect bringing the score down is how bad the courses were and the general very low academic level the university operates on. While Toronto ranks very high in the world rankings, i found it quite unacademic. The culture around education is very different abroad compared to Denmark, i had the same experience when studying at Sorbonne in Paris previously. My beef is that they do not foster autonomous or critical thinking at U of T, which i think is the main goal of Danish education, at least at HUM and SAMF (less so, but still). I really do not think that the courses i followed in Toronto live up to what I think makes an endeavour academic, which to me is sober investigation of an object(s) of interest supported by a multitude of different perspectives, methodologies and theoretical backgrounds engaged on a highly detailed level through primary texts. I.E. it needs to be 1. sober (nøgternt), 2. present multiple perspectives on the same object of interest and 3. be detailed and served through primary texts. While it might be difficult to "prove" that a course does not live up to 1 and 2, it's very easy to prove that it does not live up to 3, which none of my courses except "moral thought and behaviour" did. 

In my course "Introduction to sociology", a first year course we had no curriculum, the only thing that was expected of us between lectures was to watch a youtube playlist comprised of pop-cultural/scientific clips such as sketches from the talk show "last week tonight with John Oliver" or ted-talks. this course does obviously not live up to point 3. (i know I've created these criteria, but I would be surprised if anyone disagreed with them, except for them not being exhaustive), and it did also not really live up to criterias 1 & 2. Due to the lack of curricula and primary texts, every lecture felt like being taken along the professors train of thought, which was interesting, but in my eyes highly unacademic. There were few references to theories and if there was it was a reference to general theories (Weber's theory of Bureaucracy) and not a specific text. It all seemed as academic as a google search or a wikipedia page. The assessments were multiple choice questions about lecture content as we did not have any curricula. This results in the assessments being unacademic as they test us in content that didnt live up to the craft of academia. I remember a question from the final being "Is professor McIvor a part of the proletariat?" McIvor being our professor, and several questions about game of thrones in relation to some quasi-presentation of a sociological theory. One refutation of my critique could be that this is normal for a first year course in north america, to which i would point out that this is exactly the problem. Cause in DK we dont have levels of difficulty throughout the bachelor, we have different content, but all courses including first year are academically sound and serious. My view is that courses like this should not be possible to follow as substitutions for courses at KU, it's simply not academically a high enough level. 

In another course "Introduction to developmental Psychology," a second year course, we did have a curricula, but largely of secondary texts. Our main text book was "Twenty studies that revolutionised child psychology" in which the context and content of twenty studies is recounted. This book is valuable in that it places the studies in an academic context but very invaluable in that it was written in a style that dumbs the science of it down "to accommodate students". It's written in a convivial style, which comes of as "the professor that wants to be cool," phrases like "This sounds boring right?" were pretty common. I specifically remember when the methodology of a study by Diana Baumrind related to parenting styles  one study was presented the author simply stated that the details of the methodology were too boring and complex and would therefore not be reported on in full. This is most definitely a failure to live up to my 3rd criteria of detailed primary texts and i really think this is a disservice to us students who rather than being bombarded with a vast amount of low quality secondary texts should be offered the time to actually read and understand primary texts. The course was also fully quantitatively based with no qualitative methodology, no socio-historical perspectives, and I've never felt so far away from what we studied (child psychology) as when reviewing secondary texts about only experiments in this classroom. I do not think this course lives up to criteria 2 at all. Studies were presented as truth, and the methodology of experimentation was never questioned. The only critique "allowed" was one that already had accepted the premises of experimentation as a process of engaging truth. It was not discussed how this whole academic tradition is critiqued, how the replication crisis renders it if not invalid then at least a bit doubtful. This course also felt like being taken along the professors train of thoughts or peeping inside her brain, which could be fine it there were multiple perspectives in there, but it was more so one long argument for one specific approach. Philosophy of science does not really seems to exist in Toronto, which is a shame and a horror as this will result in a headless science charging ahead without consideration or self-reflection. Exams were also multiple choice questions, but related to curriculum or to lectures that was very closely based on curriculum. This is an improvement from Introduction to sociology.

In the course "language Acquisition", a third year course, our curriculum was also a secondary text book, but as this is within linguistics it was all very new to me, and I do not feel in a position to crtique it as with the courses above. That being said, one does not need to know the content of an academic field to be aware that the lack of primary texts and of non-experimental approaches or at least of multiple diverse approaches is needed and would improve the course.

The final course i took lives up to all criteria; "Moral thought and Behaviour" was both sober, it presented multiple perspectives, most weeks the two texts we read disagreed with each-other and they were all primary texts. This felt like a rare gem, which is horrifying as this should be the standard, as it is in copenhagen, at least at HUM, less so at Samf. the course was a seminar, so 2,5 hours out of 3 were in class discussion where we were able to ask questions, raise critiques, connect the content with out of class ideas etc. fostering autonomy and critical thinking. Some of the multiple perspectives were perspectives you would not really find in KU e.g. ethological perspectives. This specific perspective i do not really care much for, but the course really lived up to my second criteria of multiple perspectives, it was presented very soberly, and the professor was very good at accommodating and welcoming points that contradicted both him and the texts. 10/10 course
